theme: Blessed are those whose way is blameless
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:1-40. This is the first of several readings from the longest chapter in the Bible, a poem in praise of God’s word. Notice how many different words for Scripture the psalmist uses.
settingTheScene: Psalm 119 is an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, each of eight verses, with each verse in a stanza beginning with the same Hebrew letter. Nearly every verse mentions God’s word under one of several names: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, rules, word, and promise. The author is unnamed. Over the next weeks you will read it in sections, alongside Proverbs. The first stanzas describe the blessing of walking in God’s word and the psalmist’s longing to keep it.
observation: “Blessed are those whose way is blameless, who walk in the law of the LORD!” (v. 1).
“With my whole heart I seek you; let me not wander from your commandments!” (v. 10).
“How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word” (v. 9).
“I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (v. 11).
“Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (v. 18).
“I am a sojourner on the earth; hide not your commandments from me!” (v. 19).
“Turn my eyes from looking at worthless things; and give me life in your ways” (v. 37).
“I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!” (v. 32).
interpretation:
The psalm begins as Psalm 1 does, with the word “blessed.” The blessed person walks in the law of the LORD. The psalmist is not claiming to have achieved it. His prayer is that he would. He asks God to teach him, to keep him from wandering, and to open his eyes.

Verse 9 asks the question every young person faces: “How can a young man keep his way pure?” The answer is simple and demanding: guard it according to God’s word. The word is not a decoration. It is a guardrail. And verse 11 shows how: “I have stored up your word in my heart.” Memorizing and treasuring Scripture is a defense against sin. The word has to be inside to act as a guard.

Verse 18 is one of the best prayers for anyone who opens a Bible: “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law.” The psalmist knows that reading is not enough. The Spirit must open our eyes. Even a faithful reader needs God’s help to see what is there.

There is an honest strain in these verses. The psalmist feels like a sojourner, a foreigner, in the world. He asks God not to hide his commandments. He feels the pull of what is worthless, so he prays for God to turn his eyes. He knows that obedience does not come naturally.

Verse 32 offers a lovely picture: “I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart.” Obedience is not a grim trudge. When God widens the heart, it becomes a run. The psalm is not a manual of rule-keeping. It is the song of someone who has fallen in love with the voice of God.
connection: Jesus is the Word made flesh, and he is the one who perfectly walked in the law of the LORD (John 1:14; Matthew 5:17). He said, “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Ephesians 1:18 prays that “the eyes of your hearts [be] enlightened,” echoing verse 18. Colossians 3:16 urges, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.”
application:
Choose one verse to store up in your heart this week, as verse 11 urges.

Pray verse 18 before you read the Bible tomorrow.

Ask what “worthless things” your eyes are drawn to, and bring that to God.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you want to seek him with your whole heart.
Ask him to store his word in your heart so that you do not sin.
Ask him to open your eyes to wonderful things in it.
